marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q015.takeaway: Vastus medialis obliquus helps resist lateral patellar displacement by pulling the patella medially.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q015.displayText:
Vastus medialis obliquus helps resist lateral patellar displacement by pulling the patella medially.

Weakness of vastus medialis is responsible for lateral displacement of the patella.

The lowest fibres of vastus medialis attached medially to the upper half of the patella are the vastus medialis obliquus. These fibres prevent lateral patellar displacement during knee movement; weakness may cause patellar instability and pain.
emphasis: Vastus medialis obliquus helps resist lateral patellar displacement by pulling the patella medially

rationales.b: Vastus intermedius lies deep to rectus femoris and extends the knee but is not the key medial stabilizer of the patella.
rationales.c: Vastus lateralis contributes a lateral pull and does not provide the medial restraint whose weakness allows lateral displacement.
rationales.d: Rectus femoris extends the knee and flexes the hip; VMO fibers are the specific medial patellar stabilizer.

marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q016.takeaway: Semimembranosus medially rotates the flexed knee; semitendinosus and popliteus also contribute to this movement.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q016.displayText:
Semimembranosus medially rotates the flexed knee; semitendinosus and popliteus also contribute to this movement.

Medial rotation of the flexed knee is produced by semimembranosus, popliteus and semitendinosus, assisted by sartorius and gracilis.

The knee permits flexion, extension, medial rotation and lateral rotation. Flexion is by biceps femoris, semitendinosus and semimembranosus; extension by quadriceps femoris assisted by tensor fasciae latae; medial rotation of the flexed leg by popliteus, semimembranosus and semitendinosus; lateral rotation by biceps femoris.

The source notes semimembranosus tendinopathy as a cause of chronic posteromedial knee pain, especially in cyclists and marathon runners.
emphasis: Semimembranosus medially rotates the flexed knee; semitendinosus and popliteus also contribute to this movement

rationales.b: Biceps femoris laterally rotates the flexed leg at the knee, the opposite direction.
rationales.c: Quadriceps femoris extends the knee and does not produce the keyed medial rotation of the flexed leg.
rationales.d: Tensor fasciae latae acts through the IT tract to assist knee extension/stability, not medial rotation of the flexed knee.

marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q017.takeaway: Extensor hallucis longus dorsiflexes the ankle and extends the great toe; it is supplied by the deep fibular nerve.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q017.displayText:
Extensor hallucis longus dorsiflexes the ankle and extends the great toe; it is supplied by the deep fibular nerve.

The likely affected muscle is extensor hallucis longus, which is innervated by the deep peroneal nerve.
emphasis: Extensor hallucis longus dorsiflexes the ankle and extends the great toe; it is supplied by the deep fibular nerve

rationales.a: The superficial fibular nerve supplies the lateral-compartment fibular muscles and most dorsal foot skin, not EHL.
rationales.c: The tibial nerve supplies posterior-compartment plantar flexors and intrinsic sole muscles, not EHL.
rationales.d: The sciatic nerve gives rise to the deep fibular nerve, but its distal branch directly supplying EHL is deep fibular.

marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q018.takeaway: Peroneus brevis is in the lateral leg compartment; the anterior compartment contains the long toe extensors and peroneus tertius.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q018.displayText:
Peroneus brevis is in the lateral leg compartment; the anterior compartment contains the long toe extensors and peroneus tertius.

Peroneus brevis belongs to the lateral compartment of the leg.

Anterior-compartment muscles produce dorsiflexion and include extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, tibialis anterior and peroneus tertius.

Posterior-compartment muscles produce plantar flexion and are separated into superficial and deep groups. The superficial group contains gastrocnemius, plantaris and soleus. The deep group contains popliteus, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus and tibialis posterior. The lateral compartment contains peroneus longus and peroneus brevis and produces eversion.
emphasis: Peroneus brevis is in the lateral leg compartment; the anterior compartment contains the long toe extensors and peroneus tertius

rationales.b: Extensor hallucis longus lies in the anterior compartment and extends the great toe.
rationales.c: Peroneus tertius is an anterior-compartment muscle that assists dorsiflexion and eversion.
rationales.d: Extensor digitorum longus is an anterior-compartment dorsiflexor and toe extensor.

marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q019.takeaway: Peroneus longus everts and plantar-flexes the foot; tibialis anterior/posterior invert, and EHL can assist inversion.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q019.displayText:
Peroneus longus everts and plantar-flexes the foot; tibialis anterior/posterior invert, and EHL can assist inversion.

Peroneus longus is not involved in inversion; it causes eversion and plantar flexion.

Inversion elevates the medial border so the sole faces medially. Tibialis anterior causes dorsiflexion and inversion, tibialis posterior causes plantar flexion and inversion, and extensor hallucis longus extends the great toe, dorsiflexes the foot and minimally assists inversion.

Eversion elevates the lateral border so the sole faces laterally. Peroneus longus, peroneus brevis and peroneus tertius are involved. These movements occur mainly at the talocalcaneal and talocalcaneonavicular joints and partly at the transverse tarsal joint.
emphasis: Peroneus longus everts and plantar-flexes the foot; tibialis anterior/posterior invert, and EHL can assist inversion

rationales.a: Tibialis anterior dorsiflexes and inverts the foot, so it participates in inversion.
rationales.b: Tibialis posterior plantar-flexes and inverts the foot and is a strong inverter.
rationales.d: Extensor hallucis longus dorsiflexes the foot and may assist inversion.

marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q020.takeaway: Gastrocnemius contributes strongly to plantar flexion; the pictured movement is ankle plantar flexion.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q020.displayText:
Gastrocnemius contributes strongly to plantar flexion; the pictured movement is ankle plantar flexion.

The movement shown is plantar flexion of the ankle joint; weakness of gastrocnemius causes loss of this movement.

Plantar flexion is produced mainly by gastrocnemius and soleus, assisted by plantaris, tibialis posterior, flexor hallucis longus and flexor digitorum longus. Dorsiflexion is caused mainly by tibialis anterior and assisted by extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus and peroneus tertius.
emphasis: Gastrocnemius contributes strongly to plantar flexion; the pictured movement is ankle plantar flexion

rationales.a: Extensor digitorum longus extends toes and dorsiflexes the ankle rather than plantar-flexing it.
rationales.b: Tibialis anterior is the main dorsiflexor and would oppose plantar flexion.
rationales.c: Peroneus tertius dorsiflexes and everts rather than producing plantar flexion.

marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q021.takeaway: Triceps surae comprises the two gastrocnemius heads plus soleus; plantaris is a separate superficial posterior-leg muscle.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q021.displayText:
Triceps surae comprises the two gastrocnemius heads plus soleus; plantaris is a separate superficial posterior-leg muscle.

Gastrocnemius (two heads) and soleus are collectively known as triceps surae. They form a powerful muscular mass whose main function is plantar flexion of the foot.

The source notes that the main bulk of the calf is formed by gastrocnemius, plantaris and soleus, which constitute the superficial flexor group of the posterior compartment of the leg.
emphasis: Triceps surae comprises the two gastrocnemius heads plus soleus; plantaris is a separate superficial posterior-leg muscle

rationales.a: Gastrocnemius and plantaris omit soleus, which is the third head/muscle counted in triceps surae.
rationales.b: Soleus and plantaris omit gastrocnemius, whose two heads supply the 'triceps' designation.
rationales.d: Plantaris is not counted as part of triceps surae; the group is gastrocnemius plus soleus.

marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q022.takeaway: Passive dorsiflexion stretches the deep posterior compartment's flexor muscles and can provoke compartment-syndrome pain.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q022.displayText:
Passive dorsiflexion stretches the deep posterior compartment's flexor muscles and can provoke compartment-syndrome pain.

Dorsiflexion of the foot causes pain in deep posterior compartment syndrome of the leg.

All tibial fractures should be monitored for compartment syndrome; severe pain is the most important clinical feature, and swelling, blistering and skin necrosis are late features.

The source summarizes: superficial and deep posterior compartment syndromes cause pain on passive dorsiflexion of the foot and toe extension; anterior compartment syndrome causes pain on passive plantar flexion of the foot and toe flexion; lateral compartment syndrome causes pain on passive foot inversion.
emphasis: Passive dorsiflexion stretches the deep posterior compartment's flexor muscles and can provoke compartment-syndrome pain

rationales.a: Inversion does not stretch the deep posterior flexors as strongly as passive dorsiflexion.
rationales.c: Plantar flexion shortens rather than stretches the deep posterior compartment muscles.
rationales.d: Eversion is not the classic passive stretch test for deep posterior compartment syndrome.

marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q023.takeaway: The first plantar layer contains abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis and abductor digiti minimi.
marrow__ANAT_CH56_Q023.displayText:
The first plantar layer contains abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis and abductor digiti minimi.

The first layer of the sole contains abductor hallucis.

The muscles of the sole are arranged in four layers from superficial to deep. First layer: abductor hallucis, abductor digiti minimi and flexor digitorum brevis. Second layer: flexor accessorius and four lumbricals, with tendons of flexor hallucis longus and flexor digitorum longus in the same plane. Third layer: flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis and flexor digiti minimi brevis. Fourth layer: plantar and dorsal interossei and the tendons of tibialis posterior and fibularis longus.
emphasis: The first plantar layer contains abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis and abductor digiti minimi

rationales.b: Adductor hallucis lies in the third plantar layer, not the superficial first layer.
rationales.c: Flexor hallucis longus is an extrinsic leg muscle whose tendon traverses the sole; it is not a first-layer intrinsic muscle.
rationales.d: Flexor hallucis brevis belongs to the third layer of the sole.
